In the 13th century, monks at Mount Athos took apart a 6th-century copy of Paul’s letters and reused the parchment as binding material inside other books. The manuscript was scattered. Its skin got repurposed.

That book is Codex H, one of the oldest witnesses we have to Paul.

When those leaves pressed against one another, the ink left faint mirror images on the pages facing them. Ghosts of the original text, sometimes several pages deep. Invisible to the eye.

A team at the University of Glasgow just read those ghosts with multispectral imaging and recovered 42 lost pages. Radiocarbon dating in Paris supported the manuscript’s 6th-century date.

The pages carry some of the earliest known chapter lists for Paul’s letters. And they cut his letters in places that don’t match how your Bible cuts them.

The chapter numbers you read as if they were part of the text aren’t part of the text. The familiar system appeared around 1200 and is traditionally associated with an English churchman named Stephen Langton. The verse numbers came later still.

You’ve been reading a map that was drawn on top of the territory, long after the fact, by people who wanted it easier to navigate.

That obviously doesn’t make your Bible wrong. It makes the frame around it younger than you think.

And once you notice that frame, a better question opens behind it. If the divisions were added later, what did the early church see instead?
